previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with chronic headaches, hypertension, diabetes, and hyperaldosteronism was admitted due to a four-day worsening headache and a prior episode of substernal chest pressure. She presented after a clinic visit revealed severely elevated blood pressure (217/126 mmHg) and papilledema, leading to transfer from the nephrology clinic to the emergency department. Initial management included IV labetalol and hydralazine, which reduced her blood pressure. Cardiac workup, including serial troponins and EKGs, showed no evidence of myocardial infarction; chest pain was attributed to GERD given her history and normal cardiac testing. A CT head showed no hemorrhage or mass effect, with stable white matter changes. Blood pressure was stabilized with increased oral labetalol, and headache improved. She was discharged home in good condition with medication adjustments, including labetalol three times daily and a short course of oxycodone/acetaminophen for headache, along with smoking cessation counseling.

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted for further evaluation her atypical 
chest pain which was concerning initially for an acute coronary

showed the same T waves inversions and non-specific ST changes.  
The patient's chest pain was relieved promptly with one tablet 
of sublingual nitroglycerin.  The patient underwent a nuclear 
perfusion stress test which was negative for an acute coronary 
syndrome.  The patient's cardiac enzymes were negative x 3 sets. 
 The patient was discharged from the hospital in good condition. 
 It is thought that the non-specific EKG changes may be related

hypertension versus a non-cardiac cause of the chest pain.
